name: Middle cerebral artery, superior division
summary: The superior trunk of the middle cerebral artery leaves the bifurcation at the limen insulae and climbs over the frontal operculum. Its branches feed the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area on the left), the frontal eye field, the precentral and postcentral gyri for the face, hand and arm, and the anterior parietal cortex. Occlusion produces the classic 'cortical' stroke with face and arm weakness and, on the dominant side, a non-fluent aphasia.

anatomy.location: Runs upward and backward across the insula and around the frontal and anterior parietal opercula in the Sylvian fissure, emerging on the convexity as the orbitofrontal, prefrontal, precentral, central and anterior parietal arteries.

subdivisions.name: Orbitofrontal and prefrontal branches
subdivisions.note: lateral prefrontal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus

subdivisions.name: Precentral (pre-Rolandic) artery
subdivisions.note: premotor cortex, frontal eye field, Broca's area

subdivisions.name: Central (Rolandic) artery
subdivisions.note: face and arm areas of the precentral and postcentral gyri

function: Perfuses the frontal and anterior parietal convexity: motor and sensory cortex for the face, hand and arm, the frontal eye field, the premotor cortex and, on the dominant side, Broca's area.

bestView.label: central sulcus region, face and hand areas

imaging.normalAppearance: The superior trunk appears on CTA as the larger of the two M2 branches leaving the bifurcation, arching upward over the insula. Its cortical territory is the frontal and anterior parietal convexity above the Sylvian fissure.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the inferior and middle frontal gyri, precentral and postcentral gyri and anterior insula, sparing the temporal lobe and the posterior parietal cortex; the basal ganglia are spared because the lenticulostriates arise from M1.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; CTA to distinguish a branch occlusion from an M1 occlusion (which would add the lenticulostriate territory)

lesionEffects.deficit: Face and arm weakness with relative sparing of the leg
lesionEffects.mechanism: Precentral gyrus opercular and hand areas

lesionEffects.deficit: Cortical sensory loss of the face and arm

lesionEffects.mechanism: Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere

examination: Test speech output (fluency, naming, repetition) against comprehension of commands
Pronator drift and finger tapping versus hip flexion
Observe conjugate gaze deviation and test saccades to the contralateral side
pearls: Non-fluent aphasia with right face and arm weakness is the left superior division; the leg is spared and visual fields are usually intact
Comprehension is preserved because Wernicke's area belongs to the inferior division
